You must use observable credit spreads when available; when not available, you must estimate risk-neutral probabilities (not just use rating agency default rates). This also creates the DVA controversy—exit price requires DVA (own credit benefit), but monetizing it is questionable.
common_traps: Using historical default probabilities from rating agencies in CVA calculations
Thinking risk-neutral CVA is 'wrong' because credit risk is often unhedgeable
Forgetting that auditors and regulators require risk-neutral approach regardless of hedging strategy
questions.real_world_example: In 2012, a European bank calculated CVA using historical default rates (0.5% annual for BBB corporate), getting $5m CVA on a portfolio. After IFRS 13 adoption, auditors required using the counterparty's CDS spread (200bp, implying ~2% annual default probability risk-neutral). Risk-neutral CVA was $18m—forcing a $13m day-one P&L charge. The bank learned that accounting rules, not economic views, drive CVA methodology.

questions.question: In the classic bank setup (uncollateralized client trade hedged with collateralized interbank trade), what three economic costs exist beyond CVA, even when the portfolio is market-risk neutral?
questions.answer_short: The three additional costs are: (1) funding cost to post collateral on the hedge, (2) cost of capital that must be held, and (3) collateral choice optionality cost (if the counterparty can choose what to post).
questions.answer_long: Even with a perfectly hedged book (zero market risk), a bank faces: (1) FVA—when the client trade is in-the-money (positive MTM), the hedge has negative MTM requiring collateral posting that must be funded at the bank's unsecured funding rate; (2) KVA—regulatory capital must be held against both the uncollateralized client exposure and the hedged position, and capital has a cost; (3) ColVA—if collateral agreements allow the counterparty to choose what to post (currency or security type), they will choose the cheapest option, creating a cost to the receiver. Additionally, MVA exists if initial margin must be posted.
questions.why_it_matters: This framework explains why XVA desks cannot focus solely on CVA—they must manage the entire economics. A trade might have low CVA (good credit) but high FVA (large expected collateral posting) or high KVA (requires significant capital). Understanding these interconnections is essential for proper pricing, hedging, and explaining P&L to senior management.
common_traps: Thinking a collateralized hedge eliminates all costs (it creates funding cost)
Believing hedged portfolios have no counterparty risk exposure
Pricing only CVA and ignoring funding, capital, and collateral costs
questions.real_world_example: A bank executes a 10-year payer swap with an A-rated corporate (uncollateralized) and hedges with an identical receiver swap cleared at an LCH (fully collateralized with daily variation margin). CVA is low ($100k) because the corporate has good credit. However, in a rising rate scenario, the bank must post $10m collateral to LCH over 5 years, creating $3m FVA. Total XVA charge should be $3.1m, not $100k.

questions.question: Define each xVA term in simple language: CVA, DVA, FVA, ColVA, KVA, and MVA.
questions.answer_short: CVA=counterparty default cost; DVA=own default benefit; FVA=funding cost/benefit; ColVA=collateral optionality cost; KVA=cost of capital; MVA=cost of initial margin.
questions.answer_long: CVA (Credit Value Adjustment) is the expected loss from counterparty default. DVA (Debt Value Adjustment) is the benefit from your own default (controversial). FVA (Funding Value Adjustment) is the cost of funding collateral posting when out-of-the-money and benefit when in-the-money but uncollateralized. ColVA (Collateral Value Adjustment) is the cost from the counterparty's choice of what collateral to post or non-standard collateral terms. KVA (Capital Value Adjustment) is the cost of holding regulatory capital over the life of the trade. MVA (Margin Value Adjustment) is the cost of funding initial margin requirements.
questions.why_it_matters: An expert XVA practitioner must understand all components to properly price derivatives. The full price is: Basic Value - CVA + DVA ± FVA ± ColVA - KVA - MVA. Each term can be material (sometimes larger than the product's profit margin), and they interact with each other. Managing one in isolation creates unintended consequences—for example, reducing CVA through collateral creates FVA and MVA.
common_traps: Thinking XVA is just CVA (missing funding, capital, and margin costs)
Treating each XVA term independently without considering interactions
Forgetting that some terms can be benefits (DVA, sometimes FVA)
questions.real_world_example: A trader quotes a 5-year cross-currency swap to a corporate. Basic value (mid-market) is $0. CVA (counterparty default cost) is -$200k. DVA (own default benefit) is +$50k. FVA (funding cost) is -$300k. ColVA (currency choice) is -$30k. KVA (capital cost) is -$150k. MVA (initial margin cost) is -$100k. Total XVA adjustment is -$730k—the trader must charge this as an upfront fee or widen the pricing spread to break even.

questions.question: You have two swaps with a counterparty: Swap A requires you to pay $5m and receive $3m on June 15; Swap B requires you to pay $2m and receive $6m on June 15. Without payment netting, what is your settlement risk? With payment netting, what do you actually exchange?
questions.answer_short: Without netting: settlement risk is $11m (you pay $7m gross, receive $9m gross). With payment netting: you net receive $2m ([$3m + $6m] - [$5m + $2m]), settlement risk is $2m.
questions.answer_long: Without payment netting, you must pay $5m and $2m (total $7m) and separately receive $3m and $6m (total $9m). Your settlement risk is $11m total gross cashflows at risk during the settlement window. With payment netting, all cashflows on June 15 are offset: you receive net $2m = ($3m + $6m incoming) - ($5m + $2m outgoing). Settlement risk drops to just $2m. This dramatically reduces operational complexity and Herstatt-style settlement risk.
questions.why_it_matters: Payment netting is critical for operational efficiency and settlement risk reduction in OTC derivatives. Without it, dealers would have thousands of gross payments daily, creating enormous operational burden and settlement risk. XVA practitioners must ensure payment netting is legally enforceable in the relevant jurisdiction, as a failure of payment netting in default could expose the bank to massive unexpected losses.
common_traps: Assuming payment netting works across different currencies (it typically requires special provisions)
Forgetting that payment netting reduces settlement risk but not pre-settlement counterparty risk
Not confirming payment netting is legally enforceable in the counterparty's jurisdiction
questions.real_world_example: A bank has 200 interest rate swaps with a corporate counterparty, generating 50 payment dates this year with gross cashflows of $500m. With payment netting, net cashflows are only $8m. When the corporate files for bankruptcy, payment netting prevents the bank from being forced to pay gross $250m while fighting to recover their gross receivables of $258m—they only owe net $8m.

questions.question: How does close-out netting reduce counterparty risk, and why is legal enforceability critical?
questions.answer_short: Close-out netting allows offsetting all transaction values (positive and negative MTM) into a single net amount owed in default. If not legally enforceable, you must pay gross amounts owed but only receive a fraction (recovery rate) of what you're owed—catastrophic loss.
questions.answer_long: Without close-out netting, if a counterparty defaults, you must fully perform on transactions where you owe money (negative MTM) but become an unsecured creditor (receiving only recovery rate, typically 40%) on transactions where you're owed money (positive MTM). Close-out netting allows all transactions to be terminated and their MTM values offset, leaving a single net amount. Legal enforceability is critical because if a court doesn't recognize netting (due to jurisdiction or bankruptcy law), the netting agreement becomes worthless. This is why ISDA maintains legal opinions across 54 jurisdictions.
questions.why_it_matters: Close-out netting is the foundation of modern OTC derivatives markets—without it, counterparty risk would be 5-10x higher and the market couldn't exist at current scale. XVA practitioners must verify netting enforceability before trading in new jurisdictions. Post-Lehman litigation demonstrated cases where netting disputes cost hundreds of millions. Never assume netting works—confirm legal opinions exist for each counterparty jurisdiction.
common_traps: Assuming netting is automatically enforceable everywhere (it's not)
Calculating CVA with netting benefit but not confirming legal opinion exists
Forgetting that some jurisdictions have 'cherry picking' laws allowing liquidators to enforce favorable contracts while rejecting unfavorable ones
questions.real_world_example: A bank has 100 trades with a defaulting counterparty: 60 trades with +$500m total MTM, 40 trades with -$300m total MTM. Without close-out netting, the bank must pay $300m in full but only recovers 40% of $500m = $200m, netting to -$100m loss. With close-out netting, they owe net $200m and recover 40% = $80m loss. Netting saves $20m (the recovery on the offset portion).

questions.question: What are the two key differences between counterparty risk and traditional lending risk?
questions.answer_short: Counterparty risk has uncertain future exposure and is bilateral (both parties face risk), while lending risk has known notional at risk and is unilateral (only lender faces risk).
questions.answer_long: Traditional lending risk has a known notional amount at risk (like a bond near par) and only the lender faces credit risk. In contrast, counterparty risk from derivatives has highly uncertain future MTM values that can be positive or negative, and both parties face bilateral risk to each other since the contract value can swing either way.
questions.why_it_matters: This distinction fundamentally shapes how you measure, price, and manage these risks. You cannot use simple loan reserve models for derivatives - you need simulation-based exposure models and bilateral CVA calculations.
common_traps: Assuming derivative exposure equals notional (it's typically much smaller)
Thinking counterparty risk is one-sided like a loan
Not recognizing that market variables create the uncertainty in derivatives exposure
questions.real_world_example: A bank lending $100M knows its exposure is $100M. But that same bank in a $100M notional interest rate swap might have only $3M actual exposure depending on rate movements, and the counterparty also has exposure back to the bank.

questions.question: What is the difference between settlement risk and pre-settlement risk in derivatives?
questions.answer_short: Settlement risk occurs during the actual settlement period (hours/days) with exposure to full notional. Pre-settlement risk exists throughout the contract life with exposure to MTM value only.
questions.answer_long: Settlement risk arises at payment dates due to timing differences between when each party performs obligations - exposure can be 100% of notional but only for hours/days. Pre-settlement risk (counterparty risk) exists from trade date until final settlement, exposing parties to MTM differences which are typically much smaller than notional but can occur at any time during contract life.
questions.why_it_matters: These require different mitigation strategies: settlement risk needs DVP or CLS systems, while pre-settlement risk needs netting and collateral. Confusing them leads to wrong risk limits and inadequate controls.
common_traps: Ignoring settlement risk entirely because pre-settlement risk is more discussed
Treating all FX trades equally when cross-currency swaps have material pre-settlement risk
Not setting separate settlement risk limits
questions.real_world_example: Bankhaus Herstatt (1974) failed after German close but before US dollar payments went out, causing full settlement losses. This was pure settlement risk - the FX forwards themselves had little pre-settlement MTM risk.

questions.question: Why does Jon Gregory say risk mitigation is really 'risk conversion' rather than risk elimination?
questions.answer_short: Risk mitigants like netting and collateral don't remove counterparty risk - they convert it into other risks like legal risk, operational risk, liquidity risk, and increase losses to other creditors.
questions.answer_long: Netting creates legal risk if enforceability fails in a jurisdiction and increases other creditors' losses. Collateral creates operational risk (logistics), market risk (time to receive collateral), and liquidity risk (funding collateral posting). Central clearing centralizes systemic risk. Each mitigation method transforms counterparty risk into different risk types rather than eliminating it.
questions.why_it_matters: Banks that think they've eliminated counterparty risk through mitigation are dangerously naive. You must manage the NEW risks created (operational, legal, liquidity) and price them through xVA terms like FVA, MVA, and ColVA.
common_traps: Assuming collateral eliminates all counterparty risk
Not pricing the liquidity cost of posting collateral (FVA/MVA)
Ignoring legal risk in netting enforceability across jurisdictions
questions.real_world_example: Lehman Brothers was heavily collateralized, yet disputes over close-out valuation and collateral rights lasted years. The 'mitigated' counterparty risk converted into massive operational and legal risk.

questions.question: Interest rate derivatives have the largest notional outstanding but only 3.1% of that is actual market value. What does this tell you about managing IR vs equity derivative counterparty risk?
questions.answer_short: Interest rate derivatives have lower exposure per notional (3.1%) than equity (7.8%), but the massive IR notional means total IR exposure is still very significant and cannot be ignored.
questions.answer_long: The table shows IR products convert only 3.1% of notional to market value vs 7.8% for equity and 17% for commodities. However, IR notional is so large ($505T vs $8T equity) that total IR market value is actually much bigger. This means IR still dominates CVA calculations despite lower conversion rates. You need robust IR simulation models even though individual swap exposure seems small.
questions.why_it_matters: Notional is misleading for exposure estimation. A corporate with $1B IR swaps and $100M equity derivatives might actually have similar exposure levels. You must use market value or proper exposure simulation, not notional, for CVA and limits.
common_traps: Using notional as a proxy for exposure without asset class adjustments
Underestimating IR exposure because individual swap MTM looks small
Ignoring commodity derivatives because of low total notional
questions.real_world_example: A bank with $50B IR swap notional might have only $1.5B actual exposure, while $5B in commodity swaps could have $850M exposure. The commodity book requires proportionally more attention despite smaller notional.

questions.question: Why do end-users typically have directional portfolios with high MTM volatility while dealers have flat portfolios but still significant counterparty risk?
questions.answer_short: End-users hedge one-for-one economic exposures (directional), creating MTM volatility. Dealers hedge client trades (flat book) but have counterparty risk to both sides if either defaults, leaving market risk.
questions.answer_long: End-users use derivatives to hedge specific assets/liabilities (bonds issued, loans made), creating directional portfolios where MTM moves substantially with markets. Dealers intermediate - they take a client trade and hedge it, running a market-risk-flat book. However, dealers face counterparty risk bilaterally: if the client defaults, the hedge is unmatched; if the hedge counterparty defaults, the client position is unmatched. They have basis risk, not market risk.
questions.why_it_matters: This explains why end-users often don't post collateral (can't handle MTM swings) while dealers are heavily collateralized. It also shows why dealer CVA desks focus on uncollateralized client exposure even though dealers hedge everything - the asymmetry in collateralization creates the CVA problem.
common_traps: Thinking dealers have no risk because they hedge everything
Assuming end-users should collateralize like dealers do
Not recognizing that dealer risk is mainly to uncollateralized clients, not the market
questions.real_world_example: A dealer takes a 10Y receiver swap from a corporate (uncollateralized) and hedges with a payer swap to another dealer (collateralized). Rates fall 100bp. Corporate position gains $10M (no collateral posted), hedge loses $10M (dealer must post $10M cash). Dealer has funded the client's profit.

questions.question: Why might replacement cost differ significantly from mark-to-market, and when does this matter most?
questions.answer_short: Replacement cost includes bid-offer spreads, CVA/DVA, and may require non-standard replication at default. It matters most for illiquid or exotic trades and when deciding close-out amounts in default.
questions.answer_long: MTM is the present value of expected cashflows at mid-market. Replacement cost is what you actually pay to enter an equivalent transaction with a new counterparty, including bid-offer spreads, credit charges (CVA), and potentially premium for non-standard features. At default, you may face illiquid markets or need to macro-hedge rather than one-for-one replacement. Documentation references replacement cost, not MTM, which creates valuation disputes.
questions.why_it_matters: Close-out documentation uses replacement cost, which can be substantially higher than MTM for illiquid products. Lehman disputes centered on this - was exposure the mid-market MTM or the actual cost to replace? This affects CVA calculation and default loss estimates.
common_traps: Assuming MTM equals what you'll recover in default
Not adding bid-offer and CVA to MTM when estimating close-out values
Using mid-market models for close-out when you face offer-side replacement costs
questions.real_world_example: A bank has $10M MTM on an exotic structured note with a defaulted counterparty. Mid-market says $10M, but replacing it costs $12M (wide bid-offer) plus $500K CVA to the new counterparty. True loss is $12.5M, not $10M.

questions.question: What is credit exposure in counterparty risk, and why is it always calculated assuming zero recovery?
questions.answer_short: Credit exposure is the loss if the counterparty defaults (positive MTM only - you cannot gain from their default). It assumes zero recovery by convention to separate exposure from loss-given-default calculations.
questions.answer_long: Credit exposure is the loss amount conditional on counterparty default, considering that you lose the positive MTM if they owe you money, but you still owe them if MTM is negative. It's always calculated assuming no recovery by convention. Recovery is handled separately in LGD, keeping the exposure and default probability/recovery components modular in CVA calculations.
questions.why_it_matters: This separation of exposure (pre-recovery) and LGD allows you to calculate expected exposure profiles once and then apply different recovery assumptions or credit scenarios. Mixing them would require recalculating exposure for every credit assumption change.
common_traps: Multiplying exposure by (1 - recovery rate) twice - it's already built into CVA formulas
Thinking exposure should be reduced if recovery is high
Confusing gross exposure with expected loss (which includes PD and LGD)
questions.real_world_example: A $5M positive MTM swap with a counterparty has $5M exposure. CVA calculation applies PD and 40% LGD separately. If you incorrectly assumed exposure was $5M × 60% = $3M, you'd double-count recovery when computing CVA.

questions.question: Why does a high-quality counterparty tend to have increasing default probability over time while a poor-quality counterparty has decreasing forward default probability?
questions.answer_short: High-quality credits tend to deteriorate over long horizons (mean reversion), increasing forward PD. Poor-quality credits either default soon or improve (survival bias), decreasing forward PD for later periods.
questions.answer_long: For investment-grade counterparties, credit quality is expected to mean-revert downward over long time horizons, so the 10-year forward 1-year default rate exceeds the current 1-year rate. For sub-investment grade, there's high near-term default risk, but conditional on surviving (say) 10 years, their credit quality has likely improved, so forward default rates are lower. Additionally, survival probability mechanically reduces far-dated forward PD.
questions.why_it_matters: This shapes CVA profiles and credit limit structures. For good credits, long-dated exposure is riskier than short-dated (increasing PD). For weak credits, near-term exposure dominates. Assuming flat default probability over time severely misprices long-dated CVA for investment-grade names.
common_traps: Using constant annual default probability for all horizons
Not conditioning forward default rates on survival to that point
Assuming bad credits are always riskier at every tenor than good credits
questions.real_world_example: A AA-rated corporate might have 0.05% 1-year PD but 0.3% forward PD in year 10. A CCC-rated corporate has 15% 1-year PD but only 3% forward PD in year 10 (conditional on surviving). The term structure flips.

questions.question: How do credit limits work to control counterparty risk, and what is the difference between soft and hard limits?
questions.answer_short: Credit limits cap PFE to each counterparty. Soft limits block new trades that would breach the limit. Hard limits require remedial action (unwind trades, hedge) even if breached by market moves.
questions.answer_long: Credit limits set a maximum PFE (potential future exposure) allowed with each counterparty, usually varying by tenor and credit quality. New trades that breach limits are rejected. Soft limits can be breached by market movements but block further risk-increasing trades. Hard limits require immediate action like unwinding positions or hedging if breached. This controls concentration risk by diversifying across counterparties.
questions.why_it_matters: Credit limits are the first line of defense against catastrophic exposure concentration. Without them, profitable trading could lead to excessive exposure to a single counterparty. However, they're binary (yes/no) and don't optimize profitability vs risk like CVA pricing does.
common_traps: Setting limits based on notional instead of PFE
Not having escalation procedures for hard limit breaches
Making limits too tight for directional end-user clients who can't easily reverse trades
questions.real_world_example: A bank sets a $10M soft limit and $15M hard limit for a hedge fund. Market moves push PFE to $12M - no new risk-adding trades allowed. If PFE hits $15.5M, the bank must reduce exposure immediately by unwinding or hedging positions.

questions.question: What is CVA (Credit Value Adjustment) and what key inputs does it require beyond those needed for credit limits?
questions.answer_short: CVA is the market value of counterparty credit risk. Beyond PFE inputs, it requires the counterparty's default probability term structure and expected loss-given-default (LGD).
questions.answer_long: CVA quantifies counterparty risk as a dollar amount by integrating expected exposure over time against the counterparty's default probability and recovery assumptions. It requires: (1) expected exposure profile (not just PFE), (2) default probability term structure, (3) LGD assumptions, and (4) discount factors. Unlike credit limits which just cap risk, CVA prices it so you can compare risk vs return.
questions.why_it_matters: CVA transforms counterparty risk from a binary accept/reject decision to an economic pricing framework. This allows risk-adjusted profitability analysis - a trade can be above credit limits but still profitable if CVA is properly charged to the client.
common_traps: Confusing CVA (economic value) with credit reserves (accounting concept)
Using PFE instead of expected exposure for CVA calculation
Calculating CVA per trade instead of incrementally at counterparty/netting-set level
questions.real_world_example: A 10Y swap with a BB-rated corporate shows $8M PFE but only $250K CVA. The credit limit is breached but the trade is still profitable if the bank can charge the client $300K upfront, earning $50K over the cost of risk.

questions.question: Why are CVA and credit limits complementary rather than substitutes, and how do they operate at different levels?
questions.answer_short: CVA optimizes at trade and counterparty level (pricing risk, encouraging netting). Credit limits operate at portfolio level (capping concentration, encouraging diversification). Together they balance profitability and safety.
questions.answer_long: CVA works at the trade level (incorporating specific features) and counterparty level (benefiting from netting/collateral) to price risk accurately and encourage risk reduction. Credit limits work at the portfolio level to prevent excessive concentration to single counterparties or correlated groups. CVA encourages fewer counterparties (more netting), limits encourage more counterparties (diversification). Used together, CVA ensures fair pricing while limits ensure diversification.
questions.why_it_matters: Using only CVA could lead to dangerous concentration in profitable clients. Using only limits ignores profitability. Real-world practice: credit risk department approves via limits, then xVA desk prices the CVA charge - both must approve for trade to execute.
common_traps: Thinking CVA makes credit limits unnecessary
Not recognizing the tension between CVA (wants netting) and limits (wants diversification)
Failing to coordinate between credit risk and xVA desk
questions.real_world_example: A hedge fund wants a $500M notional trade that breaches the $50M limit. CVA is $5M. Credit risk denies based on limit. xVA desk could price it profitably at $6M, but limit prevents the trade - both controls working together prevent excessive concentration despite profitability.

questions.question: What is the key difference between risk-neutral and actuarial CVA, and why has the market converged on risk-neutral despite CVA being largely unhedgeable?
questions.answer_short: Actuarial CVA uses historical default probabilities (expected loss). Risk-neutral uses market-implied probabilities from credit spreads (exit price). Market uses risk-neutral due to FAS 157/IFRS 13 accounting, Basel III rules, and market practice.
questions.answer_long: Actuarial CVA treats counterparty risk like insurance - calculate expected loss using historical default rates and hold a reserve. Risk-neutral CVA uses credit spread-implied default probabilities, treating CVA as a tradeable asset with an exit price. Despite counterparty risk being illiquid and largely unhedgeable (suggesting actuarial), the market has converged on risk-neutral because: (1) FAS 157/IFRS 13 require exit pricing, (2) Basel III CVA capital is based on credit spreads, (3) market practice for novations uses spread-based CVA.
questions.why_it_matters: This is not academic - it changes CVA by 2-3x typically. Risk-neutral PDs from CDS spreads are much higher than historical PDs due to risk premium. Using historical PDs today would fail audits, violate regulations, and misprice trades relative to market. You must source credit curves, not just use rating-based historical PDs.
common_traps: Using rating-based historical default probabilities for CVA in 2024
Thinking 'unhedgeable' means you should use actuarial approach
Not understanding that IFRS 13 effectively mandates risk-neutral CVA
questions.real_world_example: A BBB corporate has 0.3% historical 5Y default probability but 1.5% CDS-implied probability. Actuarial CVA = $300K, risk-neutral CVA = $1.5M. Modern banks use $1.5M - historical approach would create $1.2M understatement rejected by auditors and regulators.

questions.question: When a derivatives dealer hedges an uncollateralized client trade with a collateralized interbank trade, what xVA components arise beyond CVA?
questions.answer_short: FVA (funding collateral on the hedge), ColVA (optionality in what collateral to post), MVA (funding initial margin), and KVA (cost of capital on both positions).
questions.answer_long: The classic dealer setup creates: (1) CVA on the uncollateralized client exposure, (2) FVA because collateral posted on the hedge must be funded (or FVA benefit on collateral received), (3) ColVA if there's optionality in currency or type of collateral posted/received, (4) MVA from funding initial margin on cleared or non-cleared margined hedges, (5) KVA because regulatory capital must be held on both the client trade and the hedge, and this capital has a cost over the trade lifetime.
questions.why_it_matters: Modern xVA desks price all these components, not just CVA. A trade might have $500K CVA but $1M FVA and $300K MVA. Pricing only CVA leaves $1.3M of real cost on the table. xVA is the total economic cost of a derivative, not just credit risk.
common_traps: Pricing only CVA and ignoring funding, collateral, and capital costs
Thinking collateralized trades have no xVA (they have FVA, ColVA, MVA, KVA)
Not recognizing that hedges create xVA costs even though market risk is flat
questions.real_world_example: Dealer takes a 10Y uncollateralized payer swap from client, hedges with collateralized receiver swap. CVA = $200K, FVA on hedge funding = $800K (must fund collateral posting if rates rise), MVA on initial margin = $400K. Total xVA charge is $1.4M, not $200K.

questions.question: If you have two swaps with a counterparty, one worth +$10M and one worth -$8M, what is your loss without netting vs with netting if they default?
questions.answer_short: Without netting: lose $10M (must still pay $8M, don't receive $10M). With netting: lose $2M (net exposure is $10M - $8M = $2M).
questions.answer_long: Without close-out netting, each transaction is separate. On default, you lose the $10M you're owed (they don't pay) but bankruptcy law still requires you to honor your $8M obligation. Total loss is $10M - $0 + $8M paid = $18M out, $0 in = $10M net loss. With netting, the two transactions combine into a single $2M net obligation owed to you. Default loss is $2M (assuming zero recovery).
questions.why_it_matters: Netting is the single most powerful counterparty risk mitigant, often reducing exposure by 80-90% for dealer portfolios. Without legal certainty of netting, the derivatives market couldn't function at current scale. This is why ISDA legal opinions on netting enforceability are critical.
common_traps: Assuming netting always works - it requires legal enforceability in the jurisdiction
Forgetting that netting applies at the netting set level, not across all counterparty trades
Not recognizing that netting increases losses to other creditors (you get paid, they don't)
questions.real_world_example: Lehman Brothers had thousands of trades with each major dealer. With netting, a dealer's net exposure might be $50M. Without netting, gross exposure could be $2B positive and $1.95B negative - losing the full $2B would have been catastrophic.

questions.question: Besides bankruptcy, what other events of default can trigger early termination and close-out under an ISDA Master Agreement?
questions.answer_short: Failure to pay/deliver, breach of agreement, credit support default, misrepresentation, default under specified transaction, cross-default, and merger without assumption can all trigger termination.
questions.answer_long: ISDA Master Agreements define multiple termination triggers beyond bankruptcy: (1) failure to pay or deliver obligations, (2) breach of agreement terms, (3) credit support default (failing to post collateral), (4) misrepresentation in documentation, (5) default under a different specified transaction, (6) cross-default (default on other obligations like bonds), (7) merger without assumption of obligations. These allow early close-out even when the counterparty hasn't technically filed bankruptcy yet.
questions.why_it_matters: Cross-default and credit support default clauses let you terminate before actual bankruptcy, potentially reducing losses. However, they can also trigger liquidity spirals - if you default on one obligation, all your counterparties can terminate simultaneously, creating a death spiral. This happened during the 2008 crisis with downgrade triggers.
common_traps: Thinking only bankruptcy triggers close-out
Not understanding that failure to post collateral is itself a default event
Ignoring cross-default clauses that can create contagion across different instruments
questions.real_world_example: Bear Stearns in March 2008 had not filed bankruptcy, but counterparties started terminating under cross-default and credit support default clauses as Bear failed to meet collateral calls. This accelerated the death spiral, forcing the JPMorgan rescue before actual bankruptcy.

questions.question: What are the two key differences between counterparty risk in derivatives and traditional lending risk in bonds or loans?
questions.answer_short: Counterparty risk has uncertain future exposure (MTM is volatile) and is bilateral (both parties have risk to each other), unlike lending where the notional is known and only one party takes risk.
questions.answer_long: In lending risk, the notional amount at risk is known with certainty (like a bond at par) and only the lender faces credit risk. In counterparty risk from derivatives, the future MTM value is highly uncertain due to market movements, and the risk is bilateral since the contract value can be positive or negative to either party. A bondholder loses if the issuer defaults, but the issuer doesn't lose if the bondholder defaults; in derivatives, either party can lose depending on who is in-the-money at default.
questions.why_it_matters: Understanding this distinction is fundamental to pricing and managing counterparty risk correctly. You cannot apply loan-style credit models directly to derivatives without accounting for MTM volatility and bilateral exposure.
common_traps: Treating derivative exposure like a fixed loan amount
Ignoring that your counterparty also has risk to you (bilateral nature)
Using only notional amounts instead of market values when assessing risk
questions.real_world_example: A bank holding a $100m bond faces $100m of credit risk. The same bank with a $100m notional interest rate swap might have only $3m of actual MTM exposure today, but this could swing to -$5m or +$8m over time depending on rate movements.

questions.question: What is the difference between settlement risk and pre-settlement risk in derivatives? Which typically has larger exposure?
questions.answer_short: Settlement risk occurs during the brief settlement period with exposure near 100% of notional. Pre-settlement risk exists throughout the life of a contract with exposure equal to replacement cost (typically much smaller).
questions.answer_long: Settlement risk arises from timing differences when payments are exchanged, exposing a party to potentially 100% of the notional for hours or days. Pre-settlement (counterparty) risk exists before contract expiration and equals the MTM replacement cost if the counterparty defaults, typically far below notional. While settlement risk has larger exposure, it exists for a much shorter time window. Pre-settlement risk is smaller but lasts the entire contract life, making default more likely.
questions.why_it_matters: Banks must manage these risks separately with different limits and mitigation strategies. Settlement risk drives the need for systems like CLS in FX markets, while pre-settlement risk drives CVA calculations and collateral requirements.
common_traps: Confusing the two types when setting credit limits
Assuming settlement risk is negligible because the time window is short
Not recognizing Herstatt risk in cross-currency settlements
questions.real_world_example: In a €1m for $1.1m FX forward, settlement risk is $1.1m on the single settlement date (you pay € but don't receive $). Pre-settlement risk might be only $50k if FX rates move from 1.10 to 1.15 during the contract life.

questions.question: Why does Jon Gregory say that risk mitigants like netting and collateral don't actually remove counterparty risk but instead convert it into other types of risk?
questions.answer_short: Risk mitigants reduce counterparty credit exposure but create operational risk (managing collateral logistics), liquidity risk (funding collateral posts), legal risk (enforceability), and market risk (collateral volatility and timing gaps).
questions.answer_long: While netting and collateral reduce credit exposure, they introduce new risks: netting creates legal risk if not enforceable in certain jurisdictions; collateral creates operational risk from daily margin calls, liquidity risk from needing to fund postings, and market risk during the time lag between exposure changes and collateral receipt. Collateral with price volatility or FX risk adds further market risk. Central clearing reduces bilateral risk but concentrates it systemically. No mitigation is free—it's risk transformation, not elimination.
questions.why_it_matters: An XVA expert must account for all costs when optimizing risk mitigation. Aggressive collateralization might reduce CVA but massively increase FVA and MVA. You need a holistic view of the total economic impact across all xVA terms.
common_traps: Thinking collateral makes counterparty risk disappear completely
Ignoring the funding and operational costs of posting margin
Not recognizing that CVA reduction might increase other xVA components
questions.real_world_example: A corporate posts $500m of collateral to reduce CVA by $10m but now faces $15m annual funding cost (FVA) and operational burden. The 'mitigation' actually increased total cost. Banks saw this acutely post-2008 when collateral demands created liquidity crises.

questions.question: An interest rate swap portfolio has $500 trillion notional outstanding but only $15.6 trillion market value (3.1% ratio). Why is market value the more relevant measure for counterparty risk?
questions.answer_short: Market value represents the actual replacement cost and potential loss in default. Notional overstates risk because swaps exchange only net cashflow differences, not principal.
questions.answer_long: Notional is misleading for counterparty risk because interest rate swaps have no principal exchange—only the difference between fixed and floating coupons is paid. The market value (sum of all future net cashflows discounted to present) represents what you'd actually lose if the counterparty defaults or what you'd pay to replace the position. This is typically 3-8% of notional depending on product type. Capital, collateral, and CVA calculations all use market value, not notional, as the basis for exposure.
questions.why_it_matters: Using notional instead of market value would massively overstate risk and capital requirements. Regulators, accountants, and risk managers all focus on market value. This is why BIS reports both figures—notional shows market size, market value shows actual risk.
common_traps: Presenting notional amounts to suggest exposure is higher than it really is
Setting credit limits based on notional rather than potential MTM
Comparing derivative exposure to bond exposure using notional
questions.real_world_example: A pension fund with $10bn notional in swaps might have only $300m actual market value at risk. If they used notional for risk assessment, they'd drastically over-reserve capital and misallocate resources across their portfolio.

questions.subtopic: End-User vs Bank Counterparty Risk Setup
questions.question: How does the counterparty risk profile differ between an end-user hedging exposures and a bank running a matched book? Why do banks face collateral asymmetry?
questions.answer_short: End-users have directional portfolios with volatile MTM, while banks hedge to be flat but face risk on both sides. Banks have collateral asymmetry: uncollateralized client trades hedged with collateralized interbank trades.
questions.answer_long: End-users typically hold directional positions to hedge business exposures (e.g., corporates hedging borrowing costs), creating significant MTM swings and collateral needs. Banks run hedged books with minimal net market risk but have counterparty risk to both clients and hedge counterparties. The key asymmetry: client trades are often uncollateralized while interbank hedges require collateral. When markets move, even though the bank's MTM nets to near zero, they must post collateral on hedges but can't collect from uncollateralized clients. This creates funding strain and is the core driver of FVA.
questions.why_it_matters: This asymmetry explains why banks charge xVA and why uncollateralized derivatives became so expensive post-crisis. Understanding this setup is essential for pricing, risk management, and explaining to clients why derivatives costs increased even when credit spreads didn't move.
common_traps: Thinking banks have no risk because their book is hedged
Ignoring the funding impact of one-sided collateral arrangements
Not recognizing that default of either client or hedge creates market risk
questions.real_world_example: A bank does a 10Y receiver swap with a corporate (uncollateralized) and hedges with a payer swap with another bank (collateralized). Rates fall 100bp. The corporate owes the bank $50m but doesn't post collateral. The bank owes $50m on the hedge and must post it immediately. The bank now has a $50m funding cost despite being MTM neutral.

questions.question: Why might the actual replacement cost of a defaulted derivative differ significantly from the pre-default MTM? What additional costs must be considered?
questions.answer_short: Replacement cost includes bid-offer spreads, liquidity costs, and potentially xVA charges from new counterparties—all of which can be substantial, especially for illiquid or non-standard products during stress.
questions.answer_long: MTM is a mid-market theoretical value, but replacing a transaction requires paying bid-offer spreads that widen dramatically in stress. Illiquid or exotic products may have no direct replacement, forcing macro hedging instead of one-for-one replication. The new counterparty will charge their own CVA and other xVA terms. Large portfolios face timing issues—replacing everything simultaneously is expensive. Documentation suggests replacement cost should include these real costs, but this creates a recursive problem since future CVA is needed to calculate today's CVA (see Section 14.6.5).
questions.why_it_matters: Underestimating replacement costs can lead to insufficient CVA reserves and unexpected losses in default. The Lehman bankruptcy showed that actual close-out costs far exceeded pre-default MTM estimates for many counterparties due to market dislocation and illiquidity.
common_traps: Assuming MTM equals replacement cost in all scenarios
Ignoring that bid-offer spreads widen massively in counterparty default
Not accounting for the new counterparty's xVA charges on replacement trades
questions.real_world_example: A portfolio with $10m mid-market MTM might cost $15m to actually replace post-default: $2m in bid-offer, $2m in CVA from the new bank, and $1m in rushed execution costs. In the Lehman default, some exotic derivatives cost 20-30% above pre-default MTM to replace.

questions.question: What is credit exposure in derivatives and why is it asymmetric (positive values matter but negative values don't)?
questions.answer_short: Credit exposure is the loss if the counterparty defaults. It's asymmetric because you lose money when you're owed (positive MTM) but still must pay when you owe (negative MTM)—you can't benefit from their default.
questions.answer_long: Credit exposure equals the positive MTM of a portfolio—what you're owed. If the counterparty defaults when you have positive MTM, you lose that amount (less recovery). If you have negative MTM, you still must honor your obligations to the bankruptcy estate and gain nothing from their default. This creates the asymmetry: exposure is max(MTM, 0). Exposure must be evaluated both today (current exposure) and in the future (potential future exposure), with future values being highly uncertain and path-dependent.
questions.why_it_matters: Understanding exposure asymmetry is fundamental to CVA pricing and risk management. It explains why options have one-sided risk and why netting is so valuable—it allows negative and positive MTMs across transactions to offset.
common_traps: Thinking negative MTM creates negative exposure (it doesn't—exposure is zero)
Ignoring that future exposure is uncertain and requires simulation
Assuming exposure is the same as MTM (it's max of MTM and zero)
questions.real_world_example: You have two swaps with a counterparty: one worth +$10m, one worth -$8m. Without netting, your exposure is $10m (you ignore the -$8m). With netting, your exposure is $2m. If they default, you lose $2m but still owe nothing because it nets.

questions.question: Why might a high credit quality counterparty have increasing default probability over time while a poor credit quality counterparty has decreasing default probability in future periods?
questions.answer_short: Good credits can deteriorate over long horizons (mean reversion), so annual default probability increases. Poor credits likely default soon or improve, so conditional annual default probability decreases.
questions.answer_long: For investment-grade counterparties, credit quality tends to mean-revert downward over time, so the probability of default in years 10-11 is higher than in years 1-2. For sub-investment grade, default is likely to happen soon if at all—if the counterparty survives to year 10, they've probably improved, making default in years 10-11 less likely than years 1-2. Additionally, the probability of surviving to the later period reduces the absolute default probability (you can't default twice). This creates term structures where good credits have upward-sloping and poor credits have downward-sloping hazard rate curves.
questions.why_it_matters: The term structure of default probability is critical for pricing long-dated CVA and setting time-dependent credit limits. Using flat default probabilities across all horizons significantly misprices risk, especially for long-dated derivatives with counterparties at quality extremes.
common_traps: Assuming default probability is constant over time
Not conditioning future default probability on survival to that point
Ignoring mean reversion in credit quality
questions.real_world_example: A AAA-rated counterparty might have 0.02% default probability in year 1 but 0.15% in year 10 (conditional on surviving). A CCC-rated counterparty might have 15% in year 1 but only 3% in year 10 conditional on surviving that long.

questions.question: How do credit limits control counterparty risk and why are they typically set to decline over time for good credit quality counterparties?
questions.answer_short: Credit limits cap the maximum potential future exposure (PFE) to each counterparty. They decline over time for good credits because long-term credit quality is expected to deteriorate (mean reversion).
questions.answer_long: Credit limits compare potential future exposure (a worst-case exposure measure, similar to VaR) against a threshold set based on the counterparty's creditworthiness. Transactions that would breach the limit are rejected. For investment-grade counterparties, limits typically decline over time because credit quality is expected to mean-revert downward—the counterparty is less reliable in 10 years than today. Limits should be conditional on survival (if they default at year 5, the year 6 limit is irrelevant). This provides diversification by preventing concentration with any single counterparty.
questions.why_it_matters: Credit limits are the first line of defense in counterparty risk management. They prevent catastrophic concentration before it happens. However, they're binary (approve/reject) and don't consider profitability, which is why CVA complements them by pricing the risk.
common_traps: Setting limits too high for long-dated exposure
Not updating limits when counterparty credit quality changes
Using limits without considering netting and collateral benefits
questions.real_world_example: A bank sets a $50m limit declining to $30m over 10 years for an A-rated corporate. A new 10Y swap would create $60m PFE at year 7, breaching the limit. The trade is rejected unless it's restructured with collateral or shorter maturity to bring peak exposure under the limit.

questions.question: What are the key advantages of using CVA instead of (or alongside) credit limits for managing counterparty risk? What does CVA account for that credit limits don't?
questions.answer_short: CVA prices the risk economically by incorporating exposure, default probability, and LGD. Unlike binary credit limits, CVA allows profitability assessment and gives credit for netting, collateral, and hedging incrementally at the counterparty level.
questions.answer_long: Credit limits are binary (approve/reject) and don't consider profitability or risk-adjusted returns. CVA quantifies the expected loss from counterparty risk by integrating exposure over time with default probability and loss given default, allowing comparison of risk and return. CVA is additive at the counterparty level and correctly accounts for netting effects and collateral incremental to existing trades. This allows profit assessment: is the revenue sufficient to cover the CVA charge? However, CVA alone doesn't prevent concentration across counterparties—hence it complements credit limits rather than replaces them.
questions.why_it_matters: CVA transforms counterparty risk management from binary gatekeeping to economic optimization. It enables the xVA desk to price risk consistently, allocate capital efficiently, and make risk/return tradeoffs. Without CVA, banks would either over-limit (losing business) or under-price (taking losses).
common_traps: Using CVA alone without credit limits (allows concentration risk)
Thinking credit limits are obsolete once CVA is implemented
Not recognizing CVA and limits work at different levels (portfolio vs counterparty)
questions.real_world_example: A bank faces a new 10Y swap with a BBB client near their credit limit. Credit limits say 'maybe' (close to limit). CVA calculation shows the incremental CVA is $500k and the client is willing to pay only $300k. The bank rejects because it's not profitable, even though within limits.

questions.subtopic: Complementary Use of CVA and Credit Limits
questions.question: Why does Jon Gregory argue that CVA and credit limits should be used together rather than CVA replacing limits? What opposite behaviors do they encourage?
questions.answer_short: CVA optimizes at the counterparty level (encourages concentration for netting benefits), while credit limits optimize at portfolio level (encourage diversification). They balance concentration vs diversification tradeoffs.
questions.answer_long: CVA calculates risk at the trade and counterparty level, benefiting from netting—it encourages concentrating trades with fewer counterparties to maximize offsetting exposures and minimize CVA. Credit limits operate at the portfolio level, capping exposure to any counterparty to avoid concentration—they encourage diversification across many counterparties. These create opposite incentives: CVA pushes toward concentration (more netting), limits push toward diversification (less catastrophic exposure). Used together, they balance economic efficiency (minimize CVA via netting) with prudent risk management (avoid concentration). The credit department approves via limits, then xVA desk prices via CVA.
questions.why_it_matters: This is fundamental to organizational structure in banks. Without both controls, you either have concentration risk blow-ups (CVA alone) or economically inefficient portfolios (limits alone). The tension between the two creates optimal risk-taking.
common_traps: Eliminating credit limits once CVA is sophisticated enough
Not recognizing the inherent conflict between netting benefits and diversification
Letting xVA desk override credit limits for profitable trades
questions.real_world_example: A hedge fund wants to concentrate all trades with one bank to minimize CVA via netting. CVA drops from $10m to $3m with concentration. But credit limits force them to split across three banks for diversification, accepting higher total CVA of $8m. This trades economic cost for reduced concentration risk—both controls matter.

questions.question: What is the difference between actuarial and risk-neutral CVA? Why has the market converged on risk-neutral despite theoretical arguments for actuarial?
questions.answer_short: Actuarial uses historical default probabilities (expected loss reserve), risk-neutral uses credit-spread-implied probabilities (market value/hedging cost). Market practice, accounting (IFRS 13), and regulation (Basel III) all mandate risk-neutral.
questions.answer_long: Actuarial CVA uses historical default probabilities and represents the statistical expected loss, treated as a reserve like loan loss provisions. Risk-neutral CVA uses market-implied default probabilities from credit spreads, representing the market value or cost to hedge. Theoretically, both have merit: derivatives use risk-neutral pricing, but credit risk is often illiquid/unhedgeable, suggesting actuarial. However, FAS 157/IFRS 13 require exit price (risk-neutral), Basel III CVA capital uses credit spreads, and major banks adopted risk-neutral first, creating market practice. The convergence happened despite the fact that CVA is rarely fully hedgeable. Historical probabilities are now almost never used.
questions.why_it_matters: This determines how you calculate CVA and whether you use bond/CDS spreads vs historical default data. Risk-neutral CVA is typically higher (credit spreads > historical defaults), so this choice materially impacts P&L, capital, and client pricing. You must use risk-neutral for compliance even if you think actuarial is theoretically better.
common_traps: Using historical default probabilities because credit is unhedgeable
Not recognizing that accounting and regulation force risk-neutral
Confusing risk-neutral (what it's worth) with actuarial (what you expect to lose)
questions.real_world_example: A BBB counterparty has 0.3% annual historical default probability but 1.2% implied from CDS spreads. Risk-neutral CVA will be 4x higher. Pre-2008, some banks used historical and took huge P&L hits when forced to move to market spreads. IFRS 13 (2013) forced European banks to switch, creating significant P&L volatility.

questions.subtopic: The Role of the CVA/xVA Desk
questions.question: What is the primary function of a CVA/xVA desk in a bank and how does it interact with trading desks and clients?
questions.answer_short: The xVA desk centralizes pricing and management of counterparty risk (and funding/capital/collateral). Trading desks transfer this risk via internal pricing, and the xVA desk manages exposure via hedging or taking risk onto their book.
questions.answer_long: The xVA desk sits between client-facing traders and the market. When a trader executes an uncollateralized client trade and hedges it with a collateralized interbank trade, they transfer the counterparty risk and funding asymmetry to the xVA desk via internal transfer pricing. The xVA desk charges the trading desk CVA, FVA, and other xVA terms, then manages the resulting exposure: they might hedge with CDS, manage collateral, or hold the risk on their book. They calculate xVA using sophisticated models and trade incrementally, considering netting with existing positions. This centralizes expertise and prevents inconsistent pricing across trading desks.
questions.why_it_matters: Without an xVA desk, trading desks would price counterparty risk inconsistently, arbitrage would emerge, and hedging would be fragmented. The xVA desk creates a single source of truth for valuation adjustments and allows holistic management of counterparty, funding, and capital costs across the bank.
common_traps: Thinking xVA desks only do CVA (they now do FVA, MVA, KVA, ColVA)
Not recognizing xVA desk should have P&L responsibility for the risk
Letting trading desks price xVA themselves (creates inconsistency)
questions.real_world_example: A derivatives trader does a 10Y uncollateralized swap with a corporate. They charge the client 50bp upfront, but the xVA desk calculates CVA + FVA = 80bp. The trading desk takes a 30bp loss on the internal transfer. The xVA desk now owns the risk and decides whether to hedge the CVA with CDS or hold it.

questions.question: Referring to Figure 4.10, explain how positive MTM, negative MTM, and flat scenarios each create different economic costs over a derivative's lifetime.
questions.answer_short: Positive MTM creates counterparty risk and funding cost. Negative MTM creates own-default benefit (DVA) and funding benefit unless collateralized. Both scenarios have capital costs and initial margin funding costs throughout.
questions.answer_long: When a derivative is in-the-money (positive MTM above threshold), you face counterparty risk (CVA) and must fund the receivable (FVA cost). The counterparty chooses what collateral to post within agreed types (ColVA). When out-of-the-money (negative MTM below threshold), you have own-default benefit (DVA) and funding benefit if uncollateralized, but if you post collateral, you choose the type and must fund it (FVA cost, ColVA). Throughout the life regardless of MTM, you bear the cost of regulatory capital (KVA) and initial margin posting (MVA). The asymmetry arises when client trades are uncollateralized but hedges are collateralized—positive client MTM creates costs without offsetting benefits.
questions.why_it_matters: This framework explains why all xVA terms exist and how they interconnect. Understanding this is essential for pricing derivatives correctly, managing funding, and optimizing capital allocation. It shows that even a 'flat' MTM position has significant lifetime costs from KVA and MVA.
common_traps: Thinking only CVA matters (ignoring funding, capital, margin costs)
Not recognizing collateral optionality has value (ColVA)
Assuming negative MTM is 'good' without considering DVA controversy
questions.real_world_example: A bank with a $100m positive MTM uncollateralized derivative faces: $2m CVA (counterparty risk), $3m FVA (funding cost), $1m KVA (cost of capital). Total xVA = $6m. If the derivative moves to -$100m, CVA becomes $0, but they now have $3m FVA benefit, $2m DVA benefit (controversial), and still $1m KVA.

questions.question: List and briefly define the six main xVA terms (CVA, DVA, FVA, ColVA, KVA, MVA) used to value OTC derivatives beyond basic risk-free pricing.
questions.answer_short: CVA (counterparty default cost), DVA (own default benefit), FVA (funding cost/benefit), ColVA (collateral optionality value), KVA (regulatory capital cost), MVA (initial margin funding cost).
questions.answer_long: CVA is the cost of counterparty default risk. DVA is the benefit from your own default (controversial). FVA captures unsecured funding costs and benefits from asymmetric collateralization. ColVA values optionality in collateral agreements (currency/type choice) and non-standard terms. KVA is the cost of holding regulatory capital over the derivative's life. MVA is the cost of funding initial margin posting (for cleared or uncleared margin rules). Together, these adjust the basic risk-free derivative value to reflect real economic costs, moving from an idealized world to actual trading reality.
questions.why_it_matters: These six terms comprise the complete economic valuation framework for derivatives post-crisis. Ignoring any component leads to mispricing. A derivatives desk must calculate all xVA terms to know the true P&L and make informed risk/return decisions.
common_traps: Thinking CVA alone is sufficient (it's not—need all six)
Confusing the terms (e.g., MVA is margin, not market value adjustment)
Not recognizing overlaps between terms (DVA vs FVA, KVA vs MVA)
questions.real_world_example: A bank prices a 10Y derivative: base value $0, CVA -$2m, DVA +$0.5m, FVA -$3m, ColVA +$0.1m, KVA -$1m, MVA -$0.5m. Total xVA adjustment is -$5.9m. The bank must charge the client this amount upfront or amortized to break even economically.

questions.question: What are the two key differences between counterparty risk and traditional lending risk?
questions.answer_short: Counterparty risk has uncertain future exposure and is bilateral, while lending risk has known notional and is unilateral.
questions.answer_long: Lending risk involves a known notional amount at risk (like a bond's par value) and only one party takes the risk (the lender). Counterparty risk differs fundamentally because the future value of derivatives is highly uncertain and depends on market variables, and both parties can have risk to each other since the MTM can be positive or negative. This bilateral nature makes counterparty risk more complex than traditional credit exposures.
questions.why_it_matters: This distinction is fundamental for XVA practitioners because it explains why derivatives require different risk management frameworks than traditional credit products. You cannot simply apply loan loss provisioning logic to derivatives—you need dynamic exposure modeling and bilateral pricing considerations like DVA.
common_traps: Thinking counterparty risk is just smaller lending risk
Ignoring the bilateral nature when pricing (forgetting DVA)
Treating notional as the amount at risk in derivatives
questions.real_world_example: A corporate buys a 10-year interest rate swap with $100M notional. Unlike a $100M loan where the full amount is at risk, the swap's exposure is only the net present value of remaining cashflows—maybe $5M today but could be $20M in 5 years or even negative. Both the corporate and the bank have risk to each other.

questions.question: What is the difference between settlement risk and pre-settlement risk in OTC derivatives?
questions.answer_short: Settlement risk occurs during the brief settlement period (hours/days) with full notional exposure; pre-settlement risk occurs before maturity with MTM exposure.
questions.answer_long: Pre-settlement risk is the risk of counterparty default before the contract matures, exposing you to the market value difference (replacement cost). Settlement risk occurs specifically during the settlement process, typically lasting hours or days, where you might pay your obligation but not receive the counterparty's payment. Settlement risk can involve 100% of notional (like in FX forwards), while pre-settlement risk involves only the MTM value which is usually much smaller.
questions.why_it_matters: Understanding this distinction helps XVA practitioners allocate risk management resources appropriately. Settlement risk requires operational controls and systems like CLS for FX, while pre-settlement risk requires exposure modeling and CVA calculations. Confusing them leads to inappropriate hedging strategies.
common_traps: Thinking all counterparty risk is the same type
Ignoring settlement risk in cross-currency trades
Not recognizing that settlement risk has higher notional but shorter duration
questions.real_world_example: In a €1M for $1.1M FX forward, settlement risk on maturity day could be the full $1.1M if you pay euros but don't receive dollars (Herstatt risk). Pre-settlement risk during the contract's life is only the MTM difference—if rates move from 1.1 to 1.15, you're exposed to $50,000, not the full notional.

questions.question: Why do risk mitigants like netting and collateral not actually remove counterparty risk, but instead convert it into other forms of financial risk?
questions.answer_short: Risk mitigants reduce CVA but create other risks like operational risk, liquidity risk, legal risk, and market risk from the mitigation mechanism itself.
questions.answer_long: Risk mitigation is really risk conversion. Netting reduces exposure but creates legal risk if enforceability fails in a jurisdiction. Collateral reduces CVA but creates operational risk (managing collateral calls), liquidity risk (funding collateral posts), and market risk (price volatility of securities posted). Central clearing reduces bilateral counterparty risk but concentrates systemic risk in CCPs and requires large initial margin. Each mitigation method has costs that appear in other xVA terms—collateral creates FVA and MVA, early termination creates MVA from liquidity buffers.
questions.why_it_matters: This concept is central to modern xVA management. A desk that reduces CVA through collateral but ignores the FVA and MVA costs is not making economically sound decisions. Optimal xVA management requires viewing all terms holistically, not optimizing one component in isolation. This is why centralized xVA desks emerged.
common_traps: Thinking collateral eliminates all counterparty risk
Ignoring funding costs when posting collateral
Not recognizing legal risk in netting agreements
Optimizing CVA without considering other xVA impacts
questions.real_world_example: A bank signs a CSA requiring daily cash collateral in the currency of each trade. This drastically cuts CVA, but now they face massive FVA costs (funding collateral posts in multiple currencies), MVA costs (if initial margin is required), and significant FX settlement risk as collateral flows back and forth. The 'solution' created new problems.

questions.question: Why is replacement cost potentially higher than mark-to-market (MTM) value, and when does this matter most for counterparty risk?
questions.answer_short: Replacement cost includes bid-offer spreads, market impact, and future xVA charges, while MTM is just present value of cashflows. This matters most in default scenarios.
questions.answer_long: MTM is the theoretical present value of remaining cashflows. Replacement cost is what you'd actually pay to enter an equivalent transaction with a new counterparty after default. This includes bid-offer spreads (which widen in stress), market impact for large positions, and crucially, the new counterparty's CVA charge (creating a recursive problem). For illiquid products, the gap can be enormous. Documentation references replacement cost, not MTM, making actual close-out amounts potentially contentious and larger than MTM suggested.
questions.why_it_matters: This gap became critical during Lehman's bankruptcy—actual replacement costs far exceeded pre-default MTM estimates. For XVA practitioners, it means exposure models using simple MTM underestimate true risk. It also creates the 'CVA recursion' problem: calculating CVA requires knowing future CVA. This is why close-out protocols and valuation disputes are so important.
common_traps: Using MTM as a proxy for actual loss in default
Ignoring bid-offer spreads in exposure calculations
Forgetting that replacement includes new CVA charges
Not accounting for illiquidity at default time
questions.real_world_example: Your 10-year exotic swap with Lehman has MTM of $10M. After default, you need replacement: the bid-offer is 200bps (not the normal 20bps) due to market stress, the new counterparty charges 150bps CVA for your credit risk, and you need to trade in size. Your actual replacement cost becomes $12.5M, not $10M. MTM was an underestimate.

questions.question: What is credit exposure in counterparty risk, and why is it time-dependent?
questions.answer_short: Credit exposure is the potential loss if the counterparty defaults, defined as the positive MTM. It's time-dependent because counterparties can default at any future time with different exposure amounts.
questions.answer_long: Credit exposure is what you would lose if the counterparty defaulted, assuming zero recovery. If MTM is positive (counterparty owes you), you have exposure equal to that amount. If MTM is negative, your exposure is zero—you can't gain from their default. Exposure is highly time-dependent because defaults can occur years in the future when market conditions are completely different. A swap that's $5M in your favor today might be $20M in your favor or zero in three years, so you must model exposure across all future dates.
questions.why_it_matters: Time-dependent exposure is the foundation of all CVA calculations. Unlike a loan where exposure is simply the outstanding balance, derivatives require sophisticated simulation of future market scenarios to determine exposure profiles. This is why CVA requires Monte Carlo simulation and cannot be calculated with simple formulas in most cases.
common_traps: Using only current MTM as exposure measure
Forgetting exposure is zero when MTM is negative
Not modeling exposure at future time points
Ignoring the asymmetry (positive MTM only matters)
questions.real_world_example: You have a 10-year receiver interest rate swap currently at par (zero MTM). Current exposure is zero, but if rates drop 200bps, exposure could be $15M. If rates rise, exposure stays zero. CVA must account for all possible future rate paths and resulting exposure profiles, not just today's zero value.

questions.question: Why does the term structure of default probability matter, and how does it differ for investment-grade versus sub-investment-grade counterparties?
questions.answer_short: Investment-grade default probability increases over time due to potential deterioration; sub-investment-grade decreases due to 'survival bias.' This affects CVA term structure.
questions.answer_long: The probability of default in any given year changes over time. For high-quality (investment-grade) counterparties, annual default probability typically increases with time because there's risk of credit deterioration. For poor-quality (sub-investment-grade) counterparties, annual default probability decreases over time—not because they improve, but because they're more likely to default early, so conditional on surviving to year 10, they've already shown resilience. This mean-reversion in credit quality is empirically observed and critically affects CVA valuation for long-dated exposures.
questions.why_it_matters: Ignoring term structure leads to significant CVA mispricing. A 20-year swap with an investment-grade counterparty has most CVA risk in the outer years when default probability is higher and exposure potentially larger. With a sub-investment-grade counterparty, most CVA risk is in early years. This affects hedging strategies—you might use 5-year CDS for IG names but shorter-dated protection for HY names.
common_traps: Using flat default probability across all years
Thinking sub-investment-grade always means higher long-term default risk
Not accounting for credit mean-reversion
Ignoring the 'survival bias' effect in long-dated CVA
questions.real_world_example: Bank A (AA-rated) has 0.05% year-1 default probability rising to 0.3% in year-10. Bank B (B-rated) has 5% year-1 default probability but only 2% year-10 (conditional on surviving 9 years). For a 10-year swap, most of Bank A's CVA comes from outer years, but Bank B's CVA is front-loaded despite similar 10-year cumulative default probability.

questions.question: What is the purpose of credit limits in counterparty risk management, and why are they typically reduced over time?
questions.answer_short: Credit limits cap maximum exposure (PFE) to any counterparty to control concentration risk. They decrease over time to account for increasing default probability for good-quality counterparties.
questions.answer_long: Credit limits set a maximum potential future exposure (PFE) allowed with each counterparty, acting as the first line of defense against counterparty risk concentration. They're set based on risk appetite and counterparty credit quality. Limits typically decrease over time because default probability for investment-grade counterparties tends to increase with horizon (though for sub-investment-grade, the opposite logic might apply). This time-dependency means a trade breaching the 5-year limit might be rejected even if it's within the 1-year limit.
questions.why_it_matters: Credit limits are essential portfolio-level risk controls that CVA calculations don't capture. CVA optimizes at the counterparty level (maximizing netting benefits), which could lead to dangerous concentrations without limits. In practice, XVA desks and credit risk teams work together—credit approves trades based on limits, then XVA prices the approved trades. Limits are binary (approve/reject), CVA provides economic pricing.
common_traps: Thinking CVA replaces the need for credit limits
Setting limits without time-dependency
Not distinguishing hard vs soft limits for market moves
Ignoring concentration risk across correlated counterparties
questions.real_world_example: A bank sets a $50M PFE limit with a hedge fund counterparty, declining to $30M after year 5. A new 7-year trade would add $25M to current $28M PFE. It's approved at year 1 (within $50M) but breaches the year-6 limit ($30M), so the trade is rejected even though CVA economics look good. Risk control trumps profit.

questions.question: What is CVA (Credit Value Adjustment) and what key components does it require beyond those needed for PFE calculation?
questions.answer_short: CVA is the price of counterparty risk. Beyond PFE components (exposure profile), it requires the counterparty's default probability and loss given default (LGD).
questions.answer_long: CVA quantifies counterparty risk as a monetary value—the expected loss from counterparty default. While PFE only needs the exposure distribution over time, CVA additionally requires: (1) the counterparty's default probability term structure, and (2) the expected loss given default (LGD). This allows CVA to price counterparty risk rather than just measuring it. CVA is calculated at the counterparty/netting-set level, accounting for all existing trades and their netting effects, making it additive across counterparties but not capturing portfolio concentration.
questions.why_it_matters: CVA transforms counterparty risk from a binary limit decision to an economic pricing decision. Rather than just asking 'does this trade fit within limits?', you ask 'is the profit sufficient to cover the CVA cost?' This enables risk-adjusted return decisions. However, CVA at counterparty level means it doesn't capture concentration risk—you need both CVA (for pricing) and credit limits (for concentration control) to manage counterparty risk properly.
common_traps: Thinking CVA captures all counterparty risk (misses concentration)
Confusing CVA with capital or PFE
Not calculating CVA incrementally with netting benefits
Using CVA without credit limits for risk control
questions.real_world_example: A bank prices a new 10-year swap with a corporate client. The standalone CVA is 120bps, but when netted with existing opposite trades, incremental CVA is only 30bps due to netting benefits. The bank charges 30bps CVA overlay on the risk-free price. However, even though CVA is low, the credit team still checks if the incremental PFE breaches limits.

questions.question: How do CVA and credit limits work together as complementary risk management tools, and what does each one optimize for?
questions.answer_short: Credit limits control portfolio-level concentration risk; CVA prices counterparty-level risk. Limits are binary risk controls; CVA enables economic pricing and risk-return decisions.
questions.answer_long: CVA and credit limits serve different but complementary purposes. CVA operates at trade and counterparty level, incorporating all trade specifics and netting effects to price counterparty risk economically—it optimizes for profit given the risk. Credit limits operate at portfolio level, preventing dangerous concentrations by capping exposures—they optimize for diversification. CVA actually encourages concentration (to maximize netting), while limits discourage it. The proper workflow is: (1) credit team checks if trade breaches limits (binary approval), (2) if approved, XVA desk prices CVA, (3) business decides if profit exceeds CVA cost.
questions.why_it_matters: Understanding this complementarity prevents two critical errors: (1) thinking CVA replaces limits, leading to dangerous concentrations, and (2) thinking limits alone are sufficient, missing proper risk-adjusted pricing. Real xVA desks work closely with credit risk teams. Major losses often occur when this coordination breaks down—either limits get overridden for 'profitable' trades, or good trades get rejected despite adequate CVA pricing.
common_traps: Using only CVA without limits (concentration risk)
Using only limits without CVA (can't make profit decisions)
Letting CVA benefits override limit breaches
Not recognizing CVA encourages concentration via netting
questions.real_world_example: A hedge fund offers a portfolio of 50 trades with excellent netting and low CVA (50bps). The desk is excited—great economics! But credit team flags that PFE will be $200M against a $100M limit, and this counterparty represents 15% of total exposure. Despite great CVA, the trade is rejected due to concentration risk. Both tools needed.

questions.question: What is the difference between risk-neutral (market-implied) and actuarial (real-world) CVA, and why has the industry converged on risk-neutral CVA?
questions.answer_short: Actuarial CVA uses historical default probabilities and represents expected loss; risk-neutral uses credit spread implied probabilities and represents market value. Industry uses risk-neutral due to accounting, regulation, and market practice.
questions.answer_long: Actuarial CVA uses historical (real-world) default probabilities and represents the expected statistical loss—common in insurance. Risk-neutral CVA uses default probabilities implied from credit spreads (CDS or bonds) and represents the market value of counterparty risk—common in derivatives. Risk-neutral probabilities are typically higher due to risk premiums. The industry has strongly converged to risk-neutral CVA driven by: (1) accounting standards (FAS 157, IFRS 13) requiring exit price, (2) Basel III CVA capital using credit spreads, (3) market practice for hedging with CDS, and (4) regulatory guidance explicitly rejecting historical-only approaches.
questions.why_it_matters: This distinction is fundamental to understanding modern CVA practice and debates. Risk-neutral CVA tends to be significantly higher than actuarial (sometimes 2-3x), affecting P&L and pricing competitiveness. It also requires liquid credit spreads, creating challenges for non-rated counterparties. The accounting requirement for DVA (own credit) under risk-neutral framework creates controversial gains when a bank's own credit deteriorates.
